To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

observers use three sources of information (heuristic, invariant 1, invariant 2) to make judgments about their heading, and that observers use these three sources in a similar way regardless of the type of motion information they see.

observers use three sources of object based information to make their heading judgments, that they are able to use this information to make accurate judgments and that they do not use motion information pooled across regions of the visual scene.

observers use object-based information, including two novel invariants, to make heading judgments and that these invariants can be used to explain the heading judgments of observers with normal and simulated peripheral vision.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of heading judgments and with how they are formed from object-based motion information.
the role of motion and spatial invariants in the perception of self-motion.
the nature of heading judgments and object motion perception in the real world.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
observers used a combination of object-based information sources to make their judgments, but did not use motion information pooled across the visual field.

observers make heading judgments from sparse forests with pursuit fixation on an object by combining the information from three object-based sources, but that the information from these three sources is used in different ways.
heading judgments are based on a combination of object-based information and pursuit fixation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
observers use all of the available information to make their heading judgments.
observers use a variety of sources of information to make heading judgments, including both local and global information.
heading judgments are based on object-based information, and that this information can be used to make accurate judgments of heading even in complex scenes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
observers can use object-based motion to guide their heading judgments even when they are not fixating on the heading-relevant object, and even in the absence of any global motion information.
observers use object-based motion information, and that the use of such information is not limited to the case of pursuit.
the heading judgments of observers in our experiments were based on object-based motion information and not on the pooling of motion across regions of the visual scene.
